# Optimizing Rebar Automation Workflows

Rhosyn Holmham: Welcome back to The Wynley Dispatch, everyone. Today we’re diving into the nitty-gritty of rebar automation workflows. I’m joined by Emrys Yarlford, lead robotics engineer at ForgeBots, who’s been pioneering the latest in rebar tying tech. Emrys, great to have you here.

Emrys Yarlford: Thanks, Rhosyn. Happy to be here and geek out on some rebar robotics.

Rhosyn: Let’s start with the basics. What’s the biggest bottleneck in current robot-assisted steel tying on construction sites?

Emrys: Honestly, it’s the variability in rebar layouts and the physical environment. Unlike a factory floor where everything’s rigid and repeatable, construction sites throw curveballs—uneven surfaces, unpredictable bar spacing, sometimes even shifting ground after a rainstorm. So the robots have to be extremely adaptable.

Rhosyn: That makes sense. You mentioned in a recent talk that sensor fusion has been a game changer. Can you explain how you’re using that in ForgeBots’ latest model?

Emrys: Sure. We combine LiDAR with ultra-wideband radio positioning and stereo cameras. The LiDAR builds a 3D map of the immediate surroundings, the stereo cameras identify bar intersections visually, and the radio beacons help counter GPS errors, especially in dense urban areas or under scaffolding. This lets the robot precisely locate where it needs to tie.

Rhosyn: I recall you sharing a story about a recent project in Wexley Heights where the robot had to handle irregular steel spacing. What happened there?

Emrys: Yeah, that was interesting. The site had some custom-designed rebar layouts—bars spaced irregularly to meet specific load criteria. The robot’s initial programming assumed uniform spacing, so it struggled. We quickly implemented an adaptive algorithm on-site. By analyzing the bar intersections in real time, the robot recalibrated its tying sequence. The result? A 30% faster tying rate than the manual crews, even with the complex layout.

Rhosyn: Impressive. What about safety monitoring—how integrated is that with the rebar robots?

Emrys: Increasingly integrated. Our current models have proximity sensors and AI-powered hazard recognition. On Wexley Heights, for example, the robot would pause tying if a human entered its immediate workspace and alert site managers if it detected loose debris or unsafe scaffolding nearby.

Rhosyn: Have you seen any resistance from crews worried about robots taking their jobs?

Emrys: Definitely, but we’ve found that when crews see the robots handling the most tedious and physically taxing tasks, like repetitive tying in cramped spaces, their attitude shifts. The robots become helpers, reducing injuries and fatigue rather than job stealers.

Rhosyn: Before we wrap, what’s next for rebar automation? Any upcoming innovations you’re excited about?

Emrys: We’re working on swarm robotics—multiple smaller bots coordinating to cover larger areas simultaneously. Plus, integrating predictive maintenance using on-board sensors to reduce downtime. It’s an exciting time.

Rhosyn: Fantastic insights, Emrys. Thanks so much for sharing your expertise.

Emrys: My pleasure, Rhosyn. Looking forward to what’s next.
